# Interpretation: Dataset spans 50 stores, 5 regions, and 20 suppliers over the period 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-31, providing broad coverage of perishable goods operations.”

# Category distribution
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = category)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Records Across Product Categories",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Region distribution
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = region)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Records Across Regions",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Quality grade distribution
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = quality_grade)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "purple") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Product Quality Grades",
    x = "Quality Grade",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Promotion status distribution
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = factor(is_promoted))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "orange") +
  labs(
    title = "Promoted vs Non-Promoted Records",
    x = "Is Promoted",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Store wise record distribution
store_counts <- original_data %>%

ggplot(store_counts, aes(x = reorder(store_id, n), y = n)) +

  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Record Distribution Across Stores",
    x = "Store ID",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# supplier wise distribution
supplier_counts <- original_data %>%

ggplot(supplier_counts, aes(x = reorder(supplier_id, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Record Distribution Across Suppliers",
    x = "Supplier ID",
    y = "Count"
  ) +

# Monthly transaction volume trend
monthly_counts <- original_data %>%
  count(month)

ggplot(monthly_counts, aes(x = factor(month), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "purple") +
  labs(
    title = "Transaction Volume by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Distribution of core business metrics
# PROFIT
original_data$profit_status <- ifelse(
  original_data$profit >= 0,
  "Profit",
  "Loss"
)
# Profit vs Loss Count Plot
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = profit_status, fill = profit_status)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Profit-Making vs Loss-Making Transactions",
    x = "Transaction Outcome",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Profit" = "steelblue", "Loss" = "tomato"))

# Binning of profit
quantile(original_data$profit, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.1))
##          0%         10%         20%         30%         40%         50% 
## -169495.000    -762.602    -149.608      12.650     125.400     276.700 
##         60%         70%         80%         90%        100% 
##     483.300     782.430    1278.072    2524.662  136195.210
original_data$profit_bucket_data_driven <- cut(
  original_data$profit,
  breaks = c(
    -Inf,
    -762.602,
    -149.608,
    125.400,
    782.430,
    2524.662,
    Inf
  ),
  labels = c(
    "Extreme Loss",
    "Moderate Loss",
    "Near Break-even",
    "Moderate Profit",
    "High Profit",
    "Extreme Profit"
  )
)

# Profit and loss segmentation plot
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = profit_bucket_data_driven, fill = profit_bucket_data_driven)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution Across Profit/Loss Segments",
    x = "Profitability Segment",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none")

original_data %>%
  count(profit_bucket_data_driven) %>%
  mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
# category wise profitability
category_profit_mix <- original_data %>%
  count(category, profit_bucket_data_driven) %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

ggplot(category_profit_mix,
       aes(x = category, y = pct, fill = profit_bucket_data_driven)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Profitability Segment Mix by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Proportion"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

avg_profit_cat <- original_data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(avg_profit = mean(profit))

ggplot(avg_profit_cat, aes(x = reorder(category, avg_profit), y = avg_profit)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Profit by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Average Profit"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Waste pct

ggplot(original_data, aes(x = waste_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "tomato",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Waste Percentage",
    x = "Waste %",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Waste by category
waste_cat <- original_data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(avg_waste = mean(waste_pct))

ggplot(waste_cat, aes(x = reorder(category, avg_waste), y = avg_waste)) +
  geom_col(fill = "orange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Waste Percentage by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Average Waste %"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Spoilage rate by category
spoil_cat <- original_data %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(spoil_rate = mean(was_spoiled) * 100)

ggplot(spoil_cat, aes(x = reorder(category, spoil_rate), y = spoil_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Spoilage Rate by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Spoilage Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Quality grade within each segment
grade_seg <- original_data %>%
  count(quality_grade, profit_bucket_data_driven) %>%
  group_by(profit_bucket_data_driven) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)

ggplot(grade_seg, aes(x = profit_bucket_data_driven, y = pct, fill = quality_grade)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = .85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("A"="#27AE60","B"="#E67E22","C"="#C0392B"),
                    name = "Quality Grade") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Quality Grade Mix Within Each Profit Segment",
       subtitle = "Grade C products are overrepresented in loss segments",
       x = NULL, y = "% within Segment") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

# Interpretation: Grade C products account for a disproportionately higher share of Extreme Loss and Moderate Loss transactions compared to their overall prevalence. This suggests that receiving lower-quality stock is a leading risk factor for profitability loss — independent of category.

# Waste % distribution by profitability segments
ggplot(original_data, aes(x = profit_bucket_data_driven, y = waste_pct, fill = profit_bucket_data_driven)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", color = "white", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Waste % by Profit Segment (Boxplot)",
       y = "Waste %", x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

# The boxplot shows a clear inverse relationship between waste and profitability. Higher waste segments have higher median waste and variability, while profitable segments show low and consistent waste levels.



# PHARMACEUTICAL PRODUCTS ANALYSIS

pharma_loss <- original_data %>%
  filter(category == "Pharmaceuticals", profit < 0)

product_loss <- pharma_loss %>%
  group_by(product_name) %>%
  summarise(total_loss = sum(abs(profit), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_loss))

top_loss_products <- product_loss %>% head(10)
options(scipen = 999)
ggplot(top_loss_products,
       aes(x = reorder(product_name, total_loss),
           y = total_loss)) +
  geom_col(fill = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top Loss-Contributing Products (Pharmaceuticals)",
    x = "Product",
    y = "Total Loss"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

    spoiled_int      = as.integer(as.character(was_spoiled))

  waste_pct ~ unsold_inventory + spoiled_int + daily_demand +
              shelf_life_days + discount_pct + temp_deviation,
  data = pharma_lm
)

# Step 3: Dropping insignificant predictors

# HYPOTHESIS TESTING

# Normality check — Anderson-Darling on a 5,000-row sample
# (full 100k makes all parametric tests reject trivially due to power)
set.seed(42)
ad_result <- nortest::ad.test(sample(original_data$waste_pct, 5000))
cat("Anderson-Darling p-value (waste_pct):", round(ad_result$p.value, 6), "\n")
## Anderson-Darling p-value (waste_pct): 0
# temperature abuse vs spoilage
# H0: Temperature abuse events have no effect on spoilage outcome
# H1: Products with more temperature abuse events are more likely to spoil
grp_sp  <- original_data$temp_abuse_events[original_data$spoiled_int == 1]
grp_ns  <- original_data$temp_abuse_events[original_data$spoiled_int == 0]
h1      <- wilcox.test(grp_sp, grp_ns)

cat("Mean (spoiled)    :", round(mean(grp_sp), 3), "\n")
## Mean (spoiled)    : 0.864
cat("Mean (not spoiled):", round(mean(grp_ns), 3), "\n")
## Mean (not spoiled): 0.786
cat("Wilcoxon W =", h1$statistic, "| p =", format(h1$p.value, scientific=TRUE), "\n")
## Wilcoxon W = 810903580 | p = 3.766358e-17
cat("DECISION:", ifelse(h1$p.value < .05,
    "REJECT H0 — temperature abuse significantly increases spoilage.",
    "FAIL TO REJECT H0"), "\n")
## DECISION: REJECT H0 — temperature abuse significantly increases spoilage.
# Mark down pricing vs waste
# H0: Markdown pricing does not reduce waste percentage
# H1: Markdown pricing significantly reduces waste %
grp_md  <- original_data$waste_pct[original_data$markdown_applied == "1"]
grp_nmd <- original_data$waste_pct[original_data$markdown_applied == "0"]
h2      <- wilcox.test(grp_md, grp_nmd)

cat("Mean waste % (markdown)   :", round(mean(grp_md), 2), "%\n")
## Mean waste % (markdown)   : 20.51 %
cat("Mean waste % (no markdown):", round(mean(grp_nmd), 2), "%\n")
## Mean waste % (no markdown): 23.51 %
cat("Reduction                 :", round(mean(grp_nmd) - mean(grp_md), 2), "pp\n")
## Reduction                 : 3 pp
cat("Wilcoxon p =", format(h2$p.value, scientific=TRUE), "\n")
## Wilcoxon p = 2.245561e-03
cat("DECISION:", ifelse(h2$p.value < .05,
    "REJECT H0 — markdown pricing significantly reduces waste.",
    "FAIL TO REJECT H0"), "\n")
## DECISION: REJECT H0 — markdown pricing significantly reduces waste.
# Interpretation:
# Waste % is not normally distributed (p ≈ 0) → non-parametric tests used
# Temperature abuse is higher in spoiled products → significantly increases spoilage (p < 0.001)
# Markdown pricing reduces waste by ~3% → statistically significant (p < 0.01)

feature_cols <- c(

  "spoilage_sensitivity","day_of_week","is_weekend","month",

)

df_model <- original_data[, c(feature_cols, "was_spoiled", "waste_pct")]
df_model <- na.omit(df_model)
cat("Model dataset:", nrow(df_model), "rows ×", length(feature_cols), "features\n")
## Model dataset: 100000 rows × 25 features
# Random forest classification model
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- createDataPartition(df_model$was_spoiled, p = .8, list = FALSE)
train_clf <- df_model[train_idx,  c(feature_cols, "was_spoiled")]
test_clf  <- df_model[-train_idx, c(feature_cols, "was_spoiled")]

cat("Train:", nrow(train_clf), "| Test:", nrow(test_clf), "\n")
## Train: 80000 | Test: 20000
cat("Class balance:\n")
## Class balance:
print(prop.table(table(train_clf$was_spoiled)))
## 
##         0         1 
## 0.8056875 0.1943125
# Only ~19.4 % of records are spoiled.
# Without balancing, a naive classifier achieves 80.6 % accuracy by
# simply predicting "Not Spoiled" always — detecting no true positives.
# ROSE (Random Over-Sampling Examples) creates a balanced training set
# through synthetic oversampling to address this class imbalance.
train_clf <- train_clf %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

test_clf <- test_clf %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

train_clf$was_spoiled <- as.factor(train_clf$was_spoiled)
test_clf$was_spoiled  <- as.factor(test_clf$was_spoiled)

library(ROSE)
## Warning: package 'ROSE' was built under R version 4.5.3
## Loaded ROSE 0.0-4
train_balanced <- ROSE(was_spoiled ~ .,
                       data = train_clf, seed = 42)$data
cat("Balanced class distribution:\n")
## Balanced class distribution:
print(table(train_balanced$was_spoiled))
## 
##     0     1 
## 39856 40144
# ntree = 200: sufficient for OOB error stabilisation
# mtry  = 5:  ~ sqrt(25 predictors), standard RF default
library(randomForest)

rf_model <- randomForest(
  was_spoiled ~ .,
  data       = train_balanced,
  ntree      = 200,

  importance = TRUE
)
print(rf_model)

# Identifying key drivers of spoilage
# Supporting EDA findings

DOCUMENTATION: 1. Objective- This analysis aims to identify the key drivers of loss in perishable goods, with a special focus on the Pharmaceuticals category. The goal is to understand whether high loss is driven by waste, spoilage, demand mismatch, or operational factors such as temperature and distribution.

  1. Data Preparation: Additional features were created to better capture operational inefficiencies:

Stock-Demand Ratio: Measures overstocking relative to demand Unsold Inventory: Captures leftover stock after sales Spoilage Indicator: Converts spoilage into numeric form for modeling

These features help in diagnosing the root causes of waste and loss. 3. Exploratory Data Analysis:

Category-Level Waste Analysis-

The heatmap shows that Pharmaceuticals have consistently high waste levels (~36–38%) across regions, indicating that the issue is category-driven rather than region-specific.

Top Loss-Contributing Products-

The bar chart highlights that Probiotics contribute the highest loss, followed by Eye Drops and Antibiotics. This suggests that certain pharma products are more prone to inefficiencies.

Waste vs Profitability-

The boxplot shows a clear inverse relationship between waste and profitability. Segments with higher waste (Extreme Loss) have higher median waste and variability, while profitable segments show low and stable waste levels.

This indicates that waste is a major determinant of profitability.

  1. Root Cause Analysis:

Regression model-

A linear regression model was used to identify the key drivers of waste.

Key Findings: Unsold Inventory has the strongest positive impact on waste Spoilage significantly increases waste Daily Demand reduces waste (higher demand = less leftover stock) Shelf Life reduces waste (longer shelf life improves sell-through) Temperature deviation has limited impact in this dataset

This confirms that waste is primarily driven by inventory and demand mismatch, rather than environmental factors.

  1. Focus Analysis: Probiotics

Probiotics show the highest loss contribution due to:

High stock relative to demand Significant unsold inventory Presence of spoilage Moderate shelf life constraints

This indicates that overstocking combined with demand mismatch is the primary reason for high losses in this category.

  1. Hypothesis Testing: A normality test (Anderson-Darling) was performed on the waste percentage.

p-value ≈ 0 The null hypothesis of normality is rejected

This indicates that the data is not normally distributed, justifying the use of non-parametric methods and machine learning models.

  1. Machine Learning Model (Spoilage Prediction): A Random Forest classification model was built to predict whether a product will be spoiled.

Steps: Data split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets Class imbalance handled using ROSE (oversampling) Model trained using multiple features including demand, temperature, and inventory

Model Evaluation ROC Curve was used to evaluate performance AUC ≈ 0.58

Interpretation: The model performs only slightly better than random, indicating limited predictive power. This suggests that spoilage may depend on additional factors not captured in the dataset.

  1. Key Insights:

Waste has a strong negative impact on profitability Overstocking is the primary driver of waste Unsold inventory is a critical contributor to loss Spoilage amplifies waste, especially in pharma products Demand plays a more important role than temperature in reducing waste High-profit segments show stable and low waste levels

  1. Recommendations

Implement demand-driven inventory planning Reduce stock levels for low-demand products Introduce dynamic pricing and early discounting to clear inventory Improve monitoring of high-risk products such as Probiotics Optimize replenishment cycles based on demand patterns

  1. Conclusion

The analysis demonstrates that waste is the primary driver of loss in perishable goods. High waste is mainly caused by overstocking and demand mismatch, which leads to unsold inventory and spoilage. Improving inventory management and aligning stock with demand can significantly reduce losses and improve profitability.
